stem:
A 28-year-old man with a 6-year history of treatment-resistant schizophrenia is due his week 12 clozapine review after commencing the medication at your community mental health team. He has tolerated titration to 300 mg nightly with a good clinical response, no sedation limiting function, and no cardiac symptoms. His weekly full blood count over the first 12 weeks has consistently shown a neutrophil count between 3.2 and 4.4 x10 to the 9 per litre (2.0-7.5).

He attends monitoring reliably and lives with his mother who supports his adherence. He has no history of febrile illness in the past week, no oral ulceration on examination, and no fever today. His electrocardiogram at week 6 was normal with a QTc of 400 milliseconds. Fasting lipids, glucose and weight are being tracked separately at the metabolic clinic.

data_table.Vital signs: within normal limits
data_table.Investigations: haemoglobin 148 g/L (130-180), white cell count 6.8 x10 to the 9 per litre (4.0-11.0), neutrophil count 4.2 x10 to the 9 per litre (2.0-7.5), platelets 240 x10 to the 9 per litre (150-400)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate frequency of full blood count monitoring from now on, assuming the neutrophil count remains in the green range?

options.text: Continue weekly full blood count monitoring indefinitely irrespective of the total duration of clozapine treatment or stable results
Extend the interval immediately to monthly full blood counts because his neutrophil count has been consistently in the safe range now
Discontinue routine haematological monitoring on the basis of a very reassuring 12-week neutrophil trend and repeat only if unwell
Switch to weekly white cell differential counts only (omit full blood count) to reduce phlebotomy burden on the patient significantly
Reduce the monitoring interval from weekly to fortnightly full blood counts and continue at that interval until the end of month 12

stem:
A 30-year-old woman with bipolar I disorder is commenced on lithium carbonate 250 mg twice daily by the community mental health team after a manic relapse successfully managed with olanzapine as inpatient. Her baseline pretreatment bloods showed a thyroid stimulating hormone of 2.2 mU/L (0.4-4.0), creatinine of 62 micromol/L (45-90) with eGFR greater than 90 mL/min/1.73 m2, calcium of 2.32 mmol/L (2.10-2.55), and a normal electrocardiogram.

She has no significant medical comorbidity and is not on any nephrotoxic medication. She has been counselled on adequate hydration, avoidance of non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs, and the early symptoms of lithium toxicity (tremor, nausea, confusion). She has effective contraception in place with a levonorgestrel intrauterine system.

data_table.Vital signs: within normal limits
data_table.Investigations: sodium 140 mmol/L (135-145), potassium 4.2 mmol/L (3.5-5.0), creatinine 62 micromol/L (45-90), calcium 2.32 mmol/L (2.10-2.55), TSH 2.2 mU/L (0.4-4.0)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate schedule of serum lithium level checks after starting therapy?

options.text: Check a random serum lithium level after 24 hours of therapy to detect early toxicity and adjust the dose against target range
Check the first level 5 to 7 days after starting or after any dose change, drawn 12 hours post-dose, then weekly until stable and 3-monthly thereafter
Do not check any serum lithium levels routinely; monitor clinically for tremor and confusion and only check if symptoms emerge
Check the first lithium level at 8 hours post-dose to capture the peak concentration and avoid missing early lithium toxicity signs
Check monthly lithium levels only after 4 weeks of therapy irrespective of any dose adjustments made in that starting period

stem:
A 29-year-old primigravid woman is reviewed at 34 weeks gestation. She has been taking sertraline 100 mg daily for major depressive disorder for the past 3 years, achieved remission before conception, and continued sertraline throughout pregnancy after a shared decision-making discussion at booking. She has remained euthymic during this pregnancy with Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale scores between 4 and 7 at each antenatal appointment. She has no anxiety symptoms and no suicidal ideation.

A colleague at another practice has suggested tapering sertraline over the next fortnight to reduce the risk of neonatal adaptation syndrome. She feels well and would prefer to continue her current dose. She has no personal history of postnatal depression and no family history of perinatal mental illness. She has strong social supports and a partner who has attended perinatal mental health education sessions with her.

data_table.Vital signs: within normal limits
data_table.Screening tools: EPDS score 6 today, no self-harm ideation, no anxiety symptoms endorsed

lead_in: What is the most appropriate recommendation about her sertraline for the remainder of the pregnancy?

options.text: Taper sertraline over 2 weeks to zero and switch to psychological therapy alone for the remainder of the pregnancy to avoid neonatal effects
Reduce the sertraline dose to 50 mg daily for the remainder of pregnancy to minimise neonatal adaptation while preserving benefit
Continue sertraline 100 mg daily at the current dose and inform the neonatal team so they can monitor for transient neonatal adaptation
Switch to fluoxetine 20 mg daily on the basis of the longest track record of use in third-trimester pregnancy studies to date
Add an intramuscular corticosteroid course now to reduce the risk of neonatal adaptation syndrome after birth by promoting neonatal maturation

stem:
A 26-year-old woman with a longstanding diagnosis of borderline personality disorder presents to a metropolitan emergency department at 11 p.m. after cutting her forearm superficially with a razor following an argument with her partner earlier this evening. The wounds are non-penetrating, have stopped bleeding after simple pressure, and do not require sutures. She has a history of six similar presentations over the past 18 months, none requiring admission.

She is engaged with a specialist BPD team and is between weekly individual dialectical behaviour therapy sessions with her regular therapist. She reports the cutting was to "stop the numb feeling" and she has no active suicidal plan or means, no current thoughts of ending her life beyond a vague chronic wish to "not exist", and she has attended tonight because her partner insisted. She is contactable, calm on interview, and denies any intent to leave against advice. She has no active psychosis, no alcohol or drug use tonight, and her regular sertraline is unchanged.

data_table.Vital signs: within normal limits
data_table.Mental state: no evidence of psychosis, mood dysphoric and reactive, judgement intact, chronic passive suicidal ideation but no acute plan or means
data_table.Wound assessment: three superficial parallel lacerations to the left volar forearm, all under 2 cm, no tendon involvement, bleeding controlled with dressing

lead_in: What is the most appropriate disposition and management plan?

options.text: Admit to an acute mental health inpatient unit for observation and weekly individual dialectical behaviour therapy while an inpatient bed
Detain under the state Mental Health Act for involuntary community treatment order for at least 3 months from today onwards
Prescribe intramuscular olanzapine 10 mg as a chemical restraint and admit to the emergency department short stay unit for the night
Discharge home with a written safety plan, contact details for her BPD team, and next-day contact from the team to arrange early review
Increase her sertraline from current dose to 200 mg daily in the emergency department as a step-up for self-harm prevention going forward

subtopic_detail: Fitness to drive on stimulant medication
stem:
A 34-year-old man is reviewed 8 weeks after commencing dexamfetamine sulfate 15 mg twice daily for newly diagnosed adult attention deficit hyperactivity disorder. He reports substantial improvement in workplace concentration and no cardiovascular symptoms. He is a private car driver only, does not hold a commercial licence, and has no history of previous crashes or driving offences. He asks whether he needs to notify the state driver licensing authority.

His blood pressure has been stable at 128/78 on treatment and his resting electrocardiogram remains normal. He has no history of substance use disorder and takes no other regular medications. He has not been advised by his psychiatrist to avoid driving. His partner and colleagues have commented that his concentration is much improved and he no longer misses turns or drifts across lanes on his commute.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse rate 76, blood pressure 128/78, respiratory rate 14, SpO2 99 percent on room air, temperature 36.7 degrees
data_table.Investigations: resting ECG normal with sinus rhythm and QTc 400 milliseconds

lead_in: What is the most appropriate advice regarding his driving?

options.text: He does not need to notify because his symptoms are well controlled on stimulant medication and he holds only a private not commercial licence class
He must cease driving entirely because stimulant medications for ADHD disqualify all patients from holding an Australian driving licence permanently
The doctor is required to notify the state driver licensing authority on the patient's behalf without informing the patient of that decision
He may continue driving without notification provided he keeps his blood pressure below 140/90 and undergoes an annual electrocardiogram
He is required to notify the state driver licensing authority himself, because untreated or treated ADHD may affect fitness to drive under the Austroads criteria

stem:
A 26-year-old woman with a history of schizophrenia is brought to the emergency department by her family after 4 days of progressive immobility. She sits motionless with her right arm held in an awkward flexed posture that she maintains for hours when placed by staff. She has not eaten or drunk voluntarily for 24 hours and has been echolalic when spoken to. She has no fever and no rigidity, and she does not resist passive movement of her limbs.

Her regular olanzapine 10 mg nightly has been unchanged for 12 months. She has no illicit drug use per her family and her urine drug screen is negative. Blood tests including full blood count, urea and electrolytes, calcium, creatine kinase and inflammatory markers are within normal limits. A non-contrast computed tomography scan of the brain is normal. Her creatinine is 62 micromol/L (45-90).

data_table.Vital signs: pulse rate 88, blood pressure 118/72, respiratory rate 16, SpO2 99 percent on room air, temperature 36.8 degrees
data_table.Investigations: creatine kinase 90 U/L (less than 200), electrolytes and calcium within normal limits, non-contrast CT brain reported as normal, urine drug screen negative
data_table.Bush-Francis catatonia rating scale: screening positive with mutism, immobility, waxy flexibility, posturing, echolalia

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial diagnostic and therapeutic step?

options.text: Administer intravenous lorazepam 2 mg and observe for improvement in mutism and posturing over the following 15 to 30 minutes as a test
Increase her olanzapine dose to 20 mg nightly on the assumption that the presentation represents worsening psychotic symptoms not otherwise
Commence subcutaneous dantrolene 1 mg/kg for suspected neuroleptic malignant syndrome pending further biochemistry results and observation
Arrange urgent electroconvulsive therapy without any pharmacological trial because ECT is the fastest treatment for catatonia in the acute setting
Perform a lumbar puncture and commence intravenous aciclovir for suspected herpes simplex encephalitis after a normal computed tomography scan

stem:
A 30-year-old woman is brought to a regional emergency department 90 minutes after an intentional overdose of her partner's amitriptyline. She has taken an estimated 40 tablets of 25 mg (approximately 1000 mg total, weight 60 kg). She was found drowsy at home but is now more alert on arrival with a GCS of 13. She has no history of ischaemic heart disease and takes no other regular medications; she has occasional migraine for which she uses paracetamol.

Initial vitals show pulse rate 128 regular, blood pressure 92/56, respiratory rate 22, SpO2 97 percent on room air, temperature 36.7 degrees. Her mucous membranes are dry. Her electrocardiogram shows sinus tachycardia at 128 with a rightward terminal R wave in lead aVR and a QRS duration of 130 milliseconds. Serum electrolytes show sodium 138 mmol/L (135-145) and potassium 3.4 mmol/L (3.5-5.0). Serum paracetamol drawn now is 15 mg/L (treatment line 150 mg/L at 4 hours). Bedside blood glucose is 5.2 mmol/L.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse rate 128, blood pressure 92/56, respiratory rate 22, SpO2 97 percent on room air, temperature 36.7 degrees
data_table.Investigations: sodium 138 mmol/L (135-145), potassium 3.4 mmol/L (3.5-5.0), bicarbonate 22 mmol/L (22-30), venous pH 7.34, QRS 130 milliseconds, terminal R wave in aVR positive, paracetamol level 15 mg/L (subtherapeutic)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Administer intravenous flumazenil 200 microgram to reverse suspected central nervous system depression from the tricyclic overdose in this case
Administer intravenous phenytoin 15 mg/kg loading dose over 30 minutes to reduce the risk of TCA-related generalised tonic-clonic seizures
Administer intravenous sodium bicarbonate 8.4 percent 1 to 2 mmol/kg bolus and repeat as needed to target a QRS width under 100 milliseconds
Administer intravenous physostigmine 2 mg to reverse the anticholinergic component of the overdose and improve mental status quickly
Administer intravenous procainamide 100 mg over 5 minutes to control tachycardia and reduce the risk of ventricular arrhythmia progression

subtopic_detail: Schizoaffective disorder versus bipolar with psychosis
stem:
A 24-year-old man is admitted with a 4-week episode of persecutory delusions (that ASIO is monitoring him), auditory hallucinations of a running commentary, elevated mood, and reduced need for sleep. He has had two prior similar admissions in the past 3 years. Careful longitudinal history taken from him and his father indicates that between admissions he has continued to hear intermittent voices and hold odd persecutory beliefs for approximately 4 to 6 weeks at a time without any prominent mood elevation, depression, or functional impairment beyond a mild degree.

Collateral confirms two prior manic episodes each lasting 3 to 4 weeks, each with prominent psychotic features, with full inter-episode return of mood to euthymia. He has been abstinent from cannabis and other substances for over 12 months, confirmed by urine drug screens. He has no family history of bipolar disorder. His current medication is quetiapine 400 mg nightly, tolerated well.

data_table.Vital signs: within normal limits
data_table.Mental state: elevated mood, pressured speech, grandiose and persecutory delusions, third-person auditory hallucinations, no cognitive impairment
data_table.Substance use: abstinent from cannabis and other substances for over 12 months, current urine drug screen negative
data_table.Collateral: between-episode auditory hallucinations and mild persecutory beliefs persist for approximately 4 to 6 weeks after mood settles

lead_in: What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.text: Bipolar I disorder with mood-congruent psychotic features because he has clear manic episodes and psychotic symptoms only during mood episodes
Schizophrenia because he has active phase symptoms of hallucinations and delusions with residual features between the acute admissions ongoing
Substance/medication induced psychotic disorder because cannabis has a very high lifetime prevalence in comorbid psychotic disorders in this age group
Schizoaffective disorder because psychotic symptoms persist for at least 2 weeks without prominent mood symptoms during the illness course overall
Brief psychotic disorder because his episodes each last less than a month and have a spontaneous resolution back to a functioning premorbid level

stem:
A 24-year-old man with first-episode psychosis has been established on olanzapine 15 mg nightly for four months. His symptoms have responded well and he has resumed his TAFE course. His weight has risen from 82 kg (BMI 26.5) at initiation to 91 kg (BMI 29.4) today.

He reports increased appetite and constant thirst but no polyuria. Baseline fasting glucose was 4.6 mmol/L and HbA1c 5.3 percent (below 5.7). He drinks alcohol two standard drinks twice a week and does not smoke. He is asking whether he should change medications.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 80/min, blood pressure 128/82 mmHg, respiratory rate 16/min, SpO2 99 percent on room air, temperature 36.6 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Weight 91 kg; waist circumference 100 cm; no acanthosis nigricans; no proximal myopathy or striae; euthymic
data_table.Investigations: Fasting glucose 5.8 mmol/L, HbA1c 6.1 percent (below 5.7), total cholesterol 5.6 mmol/L (below 5.5), triglycerides 2.4 mmol/L (below 2.0), LDL 3.5 mmol/L

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next management step?

options.text: Increase olanzapine to 20 mg nightly and re-check metabolic panel in six months
Refer to dietitian only and continue current olanzapine dose without medication change
Switch to aripiprazole with cross-titration and refer for lifestyle intervention support
Start metformin 500 mg twice daily and continue olanzapine at present dose
Cease all antipsychotic medication immediately and refer to community mental health team

stem:
A 41-year-old woman with bipolar I disorder has been on lithium carbonate 900 mg nightly for six years with excellent mood stability and no relapses. She attends for her routine annual review. Her most recent lithium level three months ago was 0.7 mmol/L (0.6 to 1.0).

She has gained 4 kg over the last year and reports feeling colder than usual, particularly in her hands. Her recent bloods show serum creatinine 92 micromol/L (baseline five years ago was 62 micromol/L), TSH 6.2 mIU/L (0.4 to 4.0), free T4 within normal limits, and corrected calcium 2.68 mmol/L (2.10 to 2.60).

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 62/min, blood pressure 128/82 mmHg, respiratory rate 14/min, SpO2 99 percent on room air, temperature 36.6 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Euthymic, no tremor, no ataxia; dry skin; delayed relaxation of ankle jerks; no palpable goitre; no peripheral oedema
data_table.Investigations: Serum lithium 0.7 mmol/L; TSH 6.2 mIU/L; corrected calcium 2.68 mmol/L; PTH 8.4 pmol/L (1.6 to 6.9); creatinine 92 micromol/L; eGFR 68 mL/min/1.73 m2

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate combined next step?

options.text: Increase lithium to 1200 mg nightly targeting 0.8 to 1.0 mmol/L range for mood stability
Stop lithium abruptly and start sodium valproate 500 mg BD for mood stabilisation
Start propranolol 20 mg twice daily for lithium-induced postural tremor management alone
Start amiloride 5 mg daily for lithium-induced nephrogenic diabetes insipidus prevention
Start levothyroxine 50 micrograms daily and refer for endocrinology review of hyperparathyroidism

stem:
A 26-year-old woman with bipolar I disorder attends for annual review. She has been well controlled on sodium valproate 1000 mg daily for two years with no admissions and no depressive or manic episodes. She has recently commenced a new relationship and asks about future family planning as her partner has raised the topic.

Her last menstrual period was two weeks ago. She uses condoms currently and is not on hormonal contraception. She has been asymptomatic and prefers to remain on valproate as it has been very effective for her.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 72/min, blood pressure 118/72 mmHg, respiratory rate 14/min, SpO2 99 percent on room air, temperature 36.7 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Alert, engaged; euthymic; no tremor or ataxia; no evidence of pregnancy
data_table.Investigations: Serum valproate 620 micromol/L (300 to 700); TSH 1.4 mIU/L; beta hCG negative today

lead_in: What is the most appropriate combined action?

options.text: Continue valproate; commence folic acid 500 micrograms daily and review annually
Continue valproate; add copper IUD and commence folic acid 5 mg daily immediately
Cease valproate abruptly today; commence quetiapine 50 mg BD titrating upward
Refer to specialist psychiatrist for pre-conception planning and switch off valproate
Halve valproate to 500 mg daily and add lamotrigine 25 mg to prepare for conception

stem:
A 27-year-old woman presents to a GP saying that she thinks she may have ADHD after her nephew was recently diagnosed. She reports lifelong difficulty finishing tasks, losing keys and wallet, chronic lateness, and needing to reread paragraphs. She dropped out of university in second year and has changed jobs six times.

She has no history of substance use, no mood disorder currently, and no previous psychiatric admissions. She holds a manual car licence and commutes 45 minutes to work daily. Her PHQ-9 today is 6 and GAD-7 is 5. She asks whether she can start medication urgently.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 80/min, blood pressure 122/78 mmHg, respiratory rate 14/min, SpO2 99 percent on room air, temperature 36.7 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Alert, engaged; no thought disorder; euthymic; no tics or motor abnormalities
data_table.Investigations: PHQ-9 6, GAD-7 5, ASRS-6 positive on 5 of 6 items; TSH 1.6 mIU/L; ferritin 48 mcg/L; iron studies within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Trial atomoxetine 40 mg oral daily now under the GP; review at four weeks
Refer to a psychiatrist for structured adult ADHD assessment before any medication trial
Trial methylphenidate immediate release 10 mg BD from the GP with driving advice
Recommend cognitive behavioural therapy alone for eight sessions before considering medication
Advise this is likely age-appropriate distractibility; reassure and review in six months

stem:
A 28-year-old man with schizoaffective disorder is brought to ED by family after four days of progressive withdrawal, mutism, and staying frozen in unusual postures. On the ward he has been observed to hold an arm in mid-air after physical positioning by the nurse and repeats phrases spoken to him. He has not eaten or drunk in 36 hours.

He was on aripiprazole 15 mg daily until two weeks ago when he self-ceased. He has had no antipsychotics since. His mother reports he had a similar episode two years ago that resolved with ECT after an unsuccessful medication trial.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 108/min, blood pressure 108/68 mmHg, respiratory rate 18/min, SpO2 98 percent on room air, temperature 37.1 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Mute, waxy flexibility on limb positioning, echolalia, staring; no rigidity or tremor; no autonomic instability
data_table.Investigations: Creatine kinase 320 U/L (below 200); electrolytes within normal limits; venous blood gas within normal limits; CT brain normal

lead_in: What is the most appropriate diagnostic and initial treatment step?

options.text: Recommence aripiprazole 30 mg oral daily targeting rapid remission of psychosis
Commence olanzapine 10 mg intramuscular now for rapid tranquillisation of psychosis
Give lorazepam 1 to 2 mg intravenous or intramuscular as a diagnostic and therapeutic challenge
Refer for emergent ECT under a mental health treatment order today as first therapy
Start haloperidol 5 mg oral three times daily and clonazepam 0.5 mg BD together

stem:
A 35-year-old man is admitted after his third manic episode with psychotic features. On this admission he had elated mood, reduced sleep for a week, grandiose delusions and pressured speech; symptoms resolved within four weeks of olanzapine and mood stabilisation. His two prior episodes were similar and both resolved with treatment.

Between episodes over the past four years he has held a stable job and had good functional recovery. Records show three months of persistent auditory hallucinations after his first admission before eventually resolving during a period of no mood symptoms. He is not currently symptomatic.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 76/min, blood pressure 122/78 mmHg, respiratory rate 14/min, SpO2 99 percent on room air, temperature 36.6 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Alert, engaged, euthymic; no formal thought disorder currently; no active psychosis on interview
data_table.Investigations: TSH 1.8 mIU/L (within normal limits); serum lithium 0.8 mmol/L (0.6 to 1.0); urine drug screen negative; MRI brain normal

lead_in: What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.text: Schizoaffective disorder bipolar type, requiring lifetime mood and antipsychotic combination therapy
Bipolar I disorder with mood congruent psychotic features during the manic episodes only
Schizophrenia with superimposed mood episodes secondary to reactive depression from illness
Substance-induced mood disorder with psychotic features from prior methamphetamine use
Brief psychotic disorder with recurrent depression and mania as separate mood diagnoses

stem:
A 34-year-old man with treatment-resistant schizophrenia has been stable on clozapine 400 mg at night for 18 months. He was admitted to a medical ward 3 days ago with community-acquired pneumonia and clozapine was withheld throughout that admission. He is now afebrile on oral antibiotics, medically stable, and has returned to the mental health unit today. He has had no seizures. His last blood monitoring 6 weeks ago showed a neutrophil count in the green range.

He is settled without acute psychotic symptoms, sleeps well and eats normal meals. He is smoking again on the unit balcony.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 82/min, blood pressure 118/74 mmHg, respiratory rate 16/min, SpO2 98 percent on room air, temperature 36.9 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Alert, oriented; no chest signs on auscultation; no meningism
data_table.Investigations: FBC neutrophils 3.4 x10^9/L (2.0-7.5), platelets 210 x10^9/L; CRP 22 mg/L (<5); ECG QTc 420 ms; clozapine last dose 72 hours ago

lead_in: What is the most appropriate approach to restarting clozapine?

options.text: Restart clozapine at the previous maintenance dose of 400 mg orally at night tonight
Restart clozapine at 12.5 mg orally at night and retitrate over 1 to 2 weeks
Restart clozapine at 200 mg orally as a single dose tonight then reassess tomorrow
Switch to oral olanzapine 20 mg nightly and cease clozapine permanently now
Delay restart until FBC monitoring is repeated and the C-reactive protein normalises

stem:
A 62-year-old woman on lithium carbonate 750 mg nightly for bipolar I disorder for 12 years presents with 3 days of coarse tremor, worsening confusion, unsteady gait and vomiting. She started a thiazide diuretic 2 weeks ago for hypertension. Her last outpatient lithium level 6 weeks ago was 0.7 mmol/L. On examination she is drowsy, moves all four limbs but is ataxic, and has hyperreflexia and myoclonic jerks.

She has no fever and no rash. She lives alone and has been unable to keep down water. Her partner brought her to hospital when she became confused overnight.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 108/min, blood pressure 96/58 mmHg, respiratory rate 22/min, SpO2 98 percent on room air, temperature 37.2 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Drowsy but rousable, GCS 13; coarse tremor and myoclonus; ataxic gait; brisk reflexes without clonus; dry mucous membranes
data_table.Investigations: Serum lithium 3.6 mmol/L (0.4-1.0); creatinine 168 micromol/L (60-110) up from 82 baseline; sodium 148 mmol/L (135-145); ECG QTc 470 ms; no ischaemic changes

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Cease lithium and give intravenous 0.9 percent sodium chloride at 200 mL/hour alone
Give activated charcoal 50 g orally and observe with 4-hourly lithium concentrations
Arrange urgent haemodialysis and cease lithium with concurrent intravenous fluids
Continue lithium at half the previous dose after starting intravenous rehydration
Give whole bowel irrigation with polyethylene glycol until effluent runs clear now

subtopic_detail: Valproate in a woman planning pregnancy
stem:
A 29-year-old woman with bipolar I disorder has been stable on sodium valproate 1000 mg daily for 4 years without relapse. She reports today that she and her partner are planning to start trying for a pregnancy in the next 3 months. She has a body mass index of 26, no other medical problems and does not smoke. Her last mood episode was a manic episode requiring inpatient admission 4 years ago.

She is euthymic today with no psychotic features. Her current supports are strong and she is engaged with a private psychiatrist and general practitioner.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 76/min, blood pressure 118/74 mmHg, respiratory rate 14/min, SpO2 99 percent on room air, temperature 36.7 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Alert, euthymic; mental state examination unremarkable; no acute risk features
data_table.Investigations: TSH within normal limits; beta-hCG negative today; LFTs within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate mood-stabiliser change?

options.text: Continue valproate at current dose and arrange preconception folate supplementation
Reduce valproate to 500 mg daily and add high-dose folate 5 mg daily orally
Cross-taper to lithium carbonate with monitoring of levels, thyroid and renal function
Cross-taper to carbamazepine 200 mg twice daily with slow monthly dose titration
Cease valproate now with no replacement and monitor for relapse with therapy alone

stem:
A 24-year-old woman is brought to ED by ambulance 90 minutes after ingesting an estimated 60 tablets of her father's amitriptyline 50 mg. She is drowsy but responsive to voice, with a widened pulse pressure and cool peripheries. Her Glasgow Coma Score is 12. Ambulance ECG en route showed a broad QRS complex.

She has a documented depressive disorder and current suicidality was declared to the paramedics. IV access has been established and 500 mL of normal saline has been infused during transport.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 128/min, blood pressure 92/56 mmHg, respiratory rate 22/min, SpO2 98 percent on room air, temperature 36.4 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Drowsy, GCS 12, dry mucous membranes, dilated pupils; abdomen soft; no focal neurological deficit
data_table.Investigations: ECG QRS 132 ms, QT 460 ms, sinus tachycardia; venous gas pH 7.30, HCO3 18 mmol/L, lactate 3.2 mmol/L; paracetamol level pending; serum tricyclic assay pending

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate treatment?

options.text: Intravenous flumazenil 0.2 mg to reverse suspected co-ingestion of benzodiazepines
Oral activated charcoal 50 g and 4-hourly repeat ECG until QRS returns to normal
Intravenous phenytoin 15 mg/kg loading dose to shorten the widened QRS
Intravenous 8.4 percent sodium bicarbonate 1 to 2 mmol/kg bolus for the widened QRS
Intravenous intralipid 20 percent 1.5 mL/kg bolus over one minute now empirically

stem:
A 38-year-old man with schizophrenia has been on olanzapine 20 mg nightly for 12 weeks after an inpatient admission for a psychotic relapse. His weight at commencement was 82 kg and today at community follow-up he weighs 91 kg. He has developed increased thirst and polyuria over the past 3 weeks. He otherwise reports good mood, no psychotic features, and has been adherent.

He smokes half a pack of cigarettes a day, drinks alcohol only socially and has no personal history of diabetes. His father has type 2 diabetes and cardiovascular disease.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 84/min, blood pressure 138/86 mmHg, respiratory rate 16/min, SpO2 99 percent on room air, temperature 36.7 degrees C
data_table.Examination: BMI 29.2; acanthosis nigricans absent; no focal neurological findings
data_table.Investigations: Random glucose 12.8 mmol/L; fasting glucose (deferred but pending); HbA1c 7.2 percent; lipids: total cholesterol 6.4 mmol/L, LDL 4.2 mmol/L, HDL 0.9 mmol/L, triglycerides 3.6 mmol/L

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management step now?

options.text: Continue olanzapine unchanged and give dietary and exercise advice at review today
Ask the patient to reduce olanzapine to 10 mg nightly with monthly HbA1c monitoring
Cease olanzapine tonight without a replacement and offer clozapine within the week
Start metformin 500 mg twice daily and continue olanzapine at the current dose
Cross-taper to aripiprazole, start metformin and refer to diabetes clinic for review

stem:
A 52-year-old man with bipolar I disorder has been maintained on lithium carbonate 900 mg nocte for 18 years with excellent mood control and no admissions in the last decade. He also takes atorvastatin 20 mg for hypercholesterolaemia. His lithium level 3 months ago was 0.7 mmol/L (0.6-1.0). His eGFR has declined progressively: 78 mL/min/1.73 m2 four years ago, 62 two years ago, and 48 today.

He is asymptomatic and works full-time. He has no polyuria, oedema or dyspnoea. Blood pressure and urinary sediment are normal. Urine albumin/creatinine ratio is 1.5 mg/mmol. He is anxious about changing his medication because his last three relapses on other agents required hospital admission. He has never taken sodium valproate and previously failed carbamazepine.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 72/min, blood pressure 124/78 mmHg, respiratory rate 14/min, SpO2 99 percent on room air, temperature 36.5 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Alert, oriented, euthymic mood, no thought disorder, no tremor, no ataxia
data_table.Investigations: Lithium level 0.7 mmol/L (0.6-1.0); eGFR 48 mL/min/1.73 m2 (progressive fall from 78); serum creatinine 128 micromol/L (60-110); urine albumin/creatinine 1.5 mg/mmol; TSH within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in his medication management?

options.text: Reduce lithium to 450 mg nocte in the community and target a serum level of 0.4 mmol/L
Continue current dose unchanged and repeat renal function testing again in 12 months
Refer to renal and psychiatric services to plan a slow lithium taper and alternative selection
Ceasing lithium abruptly to arrest the fall in renal function and starting oral olanzapine
Add amiloride 5 mg daily to preserve renal tubular function without stopping lithium therapy

subtopic_detail: Smoking cessation pharmacotherapy in a depression comorbidity
stem:
A 48-year-old man presents to your general practice wanting to quit smoking. He smokes 20 cigarettes a day, has smoked since age 18, and has failed two prior quit attempts using patches alone. He has a history of moderate major depressive disorder currently well controlled on sertraline 100 mg daily for 2 years. He has no history of cardiovascular disease, no seizure history and no active suicidal ideation.

He drinks alcohol socially (5 standard drinks a week). His BMI is 27 kg/m2 and his blood pressure is 132/82. He has never used bupropion or varenicline. He asks for the option most likely to help him quit for good this time.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 78/min, blood pressure 132/82 mmHg, respiratory rate 14/min, SpO2 98 percent on room air, temperature 36.6 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Alert, euthymic; no clubbing; chest clear
data_table.Investigations: Recent fasting lipids and BSL within normal limits; PHQ-9 = 4

lead_in: What is the most appropriate first-line pharmacotherapy?

options.text: Fluoxetine 20 mg daily instead of sertraline to help both mood and smoking cessation as the sole intervention
E-cigarettes (vaping) as monotherapy from the local vape store without prescriber involvement as the sole intervention
Varenicline titration starting at 0.5 mg once daily for 3 days, then 0.5 mg twice daily for 4 days, then 1 mg twice daily for 12 weeks
Bupropion sustained-release 150 mg once daily titrated to twice daily as sole pharmacotherapy as the sole intervention
Nicotine 21 mg/24 hour patch alone applied daily without any oral pharmacotherapy as the sole intervention

stem:
A 24-year-old woman with a 2-year history of schizoaffective disorder is brought to the psychiatric emergency service by her family after 5 days of progressive mutism and reduced oral intake. She now stares fixedly ahead, does not respond to verbal prompts, and holds her arm in the position you passively place it (waxy flexibility). She is not on any antipsychotic due to an admission gap. Family report no recent illicit drug use and no fever at home.

On examination she is afebrile with normal vital signs, no rigidity beyond the posturing described, normal reflexes and no clonus. Her serum CK is 220 U/L (55-170), U and E are within normal limits, BSL 5.2 mmol/L. A CT head performed on arrival is unremarkable. Her Bush Francis Catatonia Rating Scale on admission is 16.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 84/min, blood pressure 118/72 mmHg, respiratory rate 14/min, SpO2 99 percent on room air, temperature 36.6 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Mute; catalepsy with waxy flexibility; fixed gaze; no rigidity; deep tendon reflexes normal; no clonus
data_table.Investigations: CK 220 U/L (55-170); U and E within normal limits; BSL 5.2 mmol/L; CT head unremarkable; Bush Francis 16

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Load with IV valproate 20 mg/kg to address the mood component of her schizoaffective disorder
Recommend ECT commencement within 48 hours without a benzodiazepine challenge first
Withhold treatment and observe for 48 hours to determine spontaneous resolution first
Give IV lorazepam 2 mg with observation for 10 minutes and repeat if no partial response
Load with IV haloperidol 5 mg to break the presumed psychotic stupor immediately

subtopic_detail: Schizoaffective vs bipolar with psychotic features differentiation
stem:
A 26-year-old woman is referred to your community mental health clinic. Over the past 3 years she has had two clearly delineated episodes of elevated mood (each with reduced sleep, grandiose delusions, pressured speech, spending sprees and racing thoughts) lasting 3 weeks each, both fully resolving on quetiapine after 4 weeks of treatment. She has also had one 5 month period of persistent auditory hallucinations and paranoid delusions in the absence of any mood symptoms, occurring 6 months after her first mood episode.

Between all these episodes she has functioned well, held a stable job as a teaching assistant, and had no residual symptoms. She has no substance use disorder, no history of head injury, and no thyroid disease. She is not currently on any regular medication.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 72/min, blood pressure 118/76 mmHg, respiratory rate 14/min, SpO2 99 percent on room air, temperature 36.6 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Euthymic, reality-oriented today; no active hallucinations or delusions; cognition intact on MoCA 28/30
data_table.Investigations: Routine bloods (FBC, U and E, LFTs, TSH, B12, folate) within normal limits; urine drug screen negative

lead_in: Which diagnosis best fits her presentation?

options.text: Bipolar I disorder with psychotic features as the sole diagnosis explaining all her episodes as the sole intervention
Schizophrenia with superimposed episodes of mood disturbance as an isolated diagnosis as the sole intervention
Brief psychotic disorder recurrent type with a separate independent bipolar I diagnosis running in parallel
Delusional disorder alongside a separate diagnosis of bipolar II disorder as best fit as the sole intervention
Schizoaffective disorder bipolar type based on the 5 month psychotic period without mood symptoms plus discrete mood episodes with psychosis

subtopic_detail: Adult ADHD stimulant selection with driving occupation
stem:
A 34-year-old man is referred to your adult psychiatry service after formal assessment confirmed adult ADHD combined presentation. He has struggled with organisation, concentration and impulsivity since childhood and was untreated as a child. He works as a long-distance truck driver in New South Wales and often drives 10 hour shifts. His WURS and DIVA-5 scores support long-standing ADHD, and secondary causes have been excluded.

He has no history of psychosis, no substance use disorder, and no cardiovascular disease. Blood pressure is normal, ECG on referral is unremarkable, BMI 26 kg/m2. He is understandably concerned about maintaining his heavy-vehicle licence and asks about medication choice.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 68/min, blood pressure 122/76 mmHg, respiratory rate 14/min, SpO2 99 percent on room air, temperature 36.5 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Alert, cooperative; no tremor; cardiovascular examination unremarkable
data_table.Investigations: ECG unremarkable; TFTs, B12, folate within normal limits; DIVA-5 supports ADHD combined presentation

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial pharmacotherapy plan?

options.text: Long-acting methylphenidate (Concerta) started at low dose with formal notification to Roads and Maritime for a fitness-to-drive review before returning to driving
Dexamfetamine 5 mg twice daily commenced with a plan to continue driving during titration with routine outpatient follow-up
Atomoxetine 40 mg daily as first-line without cardiovascular considerations or driving review with routine outpatient follow-up
Bupropion sustained-release started as an off-label alternative to stimulants for immediate effect as the sole intervention
Modafinil 100 mg daily for narcolepsy-style wakefulness support without further titration with routine outpatient follow-up

stem:
A 58-year-old woman has severe recurrent major depressive disorder with three prior admissions, each requiring index ECT after failed pharmacological trials. Her most recent acute course of ECT 4 months ago produced remission after 9 treatments. She was discharged on venlafaxine 225 mg daily plus lithium 750 mg nocte. She has now presented to your outpatient clinic with re-emergent depressive symptoms (Hamilton-D 22) 3 months after the last acute ECT session and is beginning to describe passive suicidal ideation again.

She has full capacity today, is engaged in treatment planning, and has no active psychotic features. Her thyroid, B12 and folate are within normal limits. Adherence to medication has been checked and confirmed by her partner. She has no medical contraindications to further ECT.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 74/min, blood pressure 128/78 mmHg, respiratory rate 14/min, SpO2 99 percent on room air, temperature 36.6 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Depressed affect; psychomotor slowing; no psychotic features; MoCA 27/30
data_table.Investigations: TFTs, B12, folate within normal limits; venlafaxine and lithium levels therapeutic

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next intervention?

options.text: Refer for vagal nerve stimulator implantation without further trial of ECT or medication changes
Commence a course of maintenance ECT (typically weekly then tapered) alongside her current pharmacotherapy
Increase venlafaxine to 300 mg daily and add mirtazapine 30 mg nocte with no ECT plan
Switch to a monoamine oxidase inhibitor after a suitable washout without proceeding to any form of ECT
Add cognitive behavioural therapy weekly without any change to biological treatment for 12 weeks

subtopic_detail: TCA overdose management with subtle ECG changes
stem:
You are the emergency registrar at 2 am. A 22-year-old woman is brought in by ambulance 90 minutes after ingesting approximately 40 tablets of her grandmother's amitriptyline 25 mg (approximately 1 gram total). She is drowsy but rousable (GCS 13), warm and dry, and reports one episode of vomiting. She weighs 65 kg. Paracetamol level from arrival is negligible and her BSL is 5.8 mmol/L.

Her ECG shows sinus tachycardia at 122/min, QRS duration 108 ms (widening from a baseline 90 ms recorded 30 minutes ago), and QT interval 460 ms. There are no ventricular ectopics yet. Two large-bore cannulae are in place. She has not been given activated charcoal. Blood pressure is 108/64 mmHg. Anaesthetics and ICU have been paged.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 122/min, blood pressure 108/64 mmHg, respiratory rate 22/min, SpO2 98 percent on room air, temperature 36.4 degrees C
data_table.Examination: GCS 13; dilated pupils reactive to light; warm dry skin; no meningism; abdomen soft
data_table.Investigations: Paracetamol negligible; BSL 5.8; ECG QRS 108 ms (up from 90); K 3.9 mmol/L (3.5-5.2); pH 7.34, HCO3 21 mmol/L (22-32)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next intervention?

options.text: Oral activated charcoal 50 g given to a drowsy patient without airway protection right now
Physostigmine 1 mg IV to reverse the anticholinergic features seen in this presentation
IV sodium bicarbonate 100 mmol (1-2 mmol/kg) bolus and prepare for airway management as GCS deteriorates
IV flumazenil 200 microgram bolus to reverse the reduced GCS quickly as the sole intervention
IV amiodarone 300 mg over 20 minutes to treat the sinus tachycardia and prevent ventricular arrhythmia

stem:
You are the psychiatry registrar reviewing a 24-year-old man 6 months after commencing olanzapine 10 mg nightly for a first episode of schizophrenia. He is stable on the current dose with resolved positive symptoms and returning to work part time. He has gained 8 kg since starting olanzapine and his current BMI is 27 kg/m2. He has no personal history of type 2 diabetes but his father was diagnosed at age 45. He smokes 10 cigarettes daily and eats a takeaway-heavy diet.

He has had a full baseline metabolic screen before starting olanzapine including weight, waist circumference, blood pressure, fasting lipids, fasting glucose and prolactin. He now attends for routine follow up. He would like to continue olanzapine as it has clearly helped his symptoms and asks what monitoring he should have.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 78/min, blood pressure 132/84 mmHg, respiratory rate 14/min, SpO2 99 percent on room air, temperature 36.6 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Weight 92 kg, waist circumference 98 cm, no extrapyramidal signs
data_table.Investigations: Baseline (6 months ago): fasting glucose 4.8 mmol/L, HbA1c 5.4 percent, total cholesterol 4.8 mmol/L, triglycerides 1.4 mmol/L, prolactin 320 mIU/L (<430)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate metabolic monitoring plan for this patient?

options.text: Fasting lipids, fasting glucose and HbA1c annually; weight and blood pressure at each mental state review
Fasting lipids, glucose and HbA1c now and again at 12 months, then annually; weight and BP each visit
Cease olanzapine now and switch to aripiprazole because weight gain of over 5 kg mandates change
Repeat only prolactin and ECG now, deferring metabolic bloods until 12 months post-initiation
Refer to endocrinology for glucose tolerance test now regardless of the current fasting glucose result today

stem:
A 42-year-old woman with bipolar I disorder has been on lithium carbonate 750 mg nightly for 5 years with excellent mood stability. She has had no manic or depressive relapses in that time. Her last set of monitoring bloods 12 months ago showed lithium level 0.7 mmol/L (0.6-0.8), TSH 2.4 mIU/L (0.4-4.0), creatinine 78 micromol/L (45-90) and calcium 2.32 mmol/L (2.15-2.60). She attends your outpatient clinic for routine review; she has no symptoms of toxicity, no polyuria and no cognitive concerns.

She takes no other medications, does not smoke and drinks no alcohol. She is on a stable diet with regular fluid intake. There is no personal or family history of thyroid disease. She would like to know what long-term monitoring is required from here on.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 72/min, blood pressure 118/74 mmHg, respiratory rate 14/min, SpO2 99 percent on room air, temperature 36.6 degrees C
data_table.Examination: No tremor, no cognitive impairment, no goitre, no oedema
data_table.Investigations: 12 months ago: lithium 0.7 mmol/L; TSH 2.4 mIU/L; creatinine 78 micromol/L; calcium 2.32 mmol/L; today's clinical review only

lead_in: What is the most appropriate ongoing monitoring plan?

options.text: Check lithium level annually; renal, thyroid and parathyroid function only if symptoms of derangement develop
Repeat lithium level, urea and electrolytes, calcium and thyroid function tests every 3 months for the next year
Repeat lithium level, urea and electrolytes, calcium and thyroid function every 6 months as long as she remains stable
Cease lithium and switch to sodium valproate to avoid further renal exposure risk in the coming years
Add annual glomerular filtration rate estimate but omit thyroid function tests because she is asymptomatic

stem:
A 24-year-old woman with bipolar I disorder is stable on sodium valproate 1000 mg daily for the last 3 years after two hospitalisations for mania in her early 20s. She and her new partner have started discussing having a baby in the next 12 months. She currently uses no contraception and denies missed periods. Prior trials of lithium caused unacceptable tremor and cognitive slowing, and olanzapine caused significant weight gain. She has never been trialled on lamotrigine.

On examination she is euthymic with good insight. She has no active suicidal ideation. She is well engaged with her community mental health team. Her most recent valproate level was 550 micromol/L (300-700), FBC, LFTs and pregnancy test today are normal. She reads widely and asks specifically about the risks of continuing valproate through pregnancy.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 74/min, blood pressure 116/72 mmHg, respiratory rate 14/min, SpO2 99 percent on room air, temperature 36.6 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Euthymic, good insight, no suicidal or homicidal ideation
data_table.Investigations: Valproate 550 micromol/L (300-700); full blood count within normal limits; liver function tests within normal limits; beta hCG negative today

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management plan?

options.text: Continue valproate at current dose through pregnancy because the mood benefits outweigh teratogenic risk for a stable patient
Halve valproate dose to 500 mg daily immediately to reduce dose-dependent teratogenicity and continue conception planning
Add 5 mg folate daily and continue valproate through the first trimester to reduce neural tube defect risk
Ensure reliable contraception, plan cross-titration to lamotrigine before conception, and start 5 mg folate daily
Cease valproate abruptly today and monitor mood over the next 4 to 6 weeks without any bridging medication or plan

subtopic_detail: Treating a refusing patient after life-threatening self-poisoning
stem: A 45-year-old man in a Sydney emergency department took amitriptyline two hours ago. He is drowsy, pulls at his cannula and says he wants to be left to die. He is not a detained patient and his blood pressure is falling.

data_table.ECG: Sinus tachycardia, QRS 122 ms and widening
data_table.Examination: GCS 12, dry skin, dilated pupils, no focal deficit

lead_in: What is the most appropriate course of action?

options.text: Provide urgent treatment without consent as an emergency
Detain and treat him under the NSW Mental Health Act 2007
Await a psychiatry opinion before any further treatment
Accept his stated refusal and give comfort measures
Obtain written consent from his nearest relative first

subtopic_detail: Schizoaffective disorder vs bipolar I with psychotic features
stem:
You are the community psychiatry registrar reviewing a 26-year-old man for a diagnostic clarification. Over the last 3 years he has had three admissions. The first was for a manic episode with grandiose delusions and severe overspending, lasting 8 weeks, with delusions resolving as mood stabilised on lithium and olanzapine. The second was a severe depressive episode with psychomotor retardation and mood-congruent nihilistic delusions, resolving with ECT and antidepressant. The third, six months ago, was for two weeks of persecutory delusions and auditory hallucinations occurring in the setting of euthymic mood and no sleep or energy changes, resolving on aripiprazole.

Between episodes he has been employed part time as a barista, socially engaged with friends, and adherent to olanzapine 10 mg with lithium 900 mg. His mother has bipolar I disorder. He denies substance use and a urine drug screen has consistently been negative. There are no autism spectrum, developmental or intellectual disability features. Insight into the illness is good.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 74/min, blood pressure 118/72 mmHg, respiratory rate 14/min, SpO2 99 percent on room air, temperature 36.7 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Currently euthymic, no active psychotic symptoms, good insight
data_table.Investigations: Urine drug screen negative on multiple occasions; TFT, UEC and lithium level within normal limits

lead_in: Which single diagnosis best explains his clinical course?

options.text: Schizoaffective disorder bipolar type based on the presence of psychotic symptoms without concurrent mood disturbance
Bipolar I disorder with psychotic features that only occur during mood episodes across all presentations
Schizophrenia with concurrent depressive symptoms and comorbid mood-related admissions but no true bipolarity
Substance-induced psychotic disorder because acute psychotic episodes commonly follow cannabis or amphetamine use
Delusional disorder because persecutory delusions occurred without hallucinations or mood disturbance in the third episode

stem:
You are the psychiatry registrar assessing a 19-year-old man on the acute mental health inpatient unit day 3 post-admission. He was brought by police 3 days ago after climbing a construction crane in central Melbourne responding to voices telling him to warn the city about surveillance. His mother reports daily heavy use of high-potency skunk cannabis for the past 2 years and heavier use in the fortnight before admission after his relationship ended. Urine drug screen on admission was positive for cannabinoids only; alcohol, amphetamines and cocaine were negative.

On assessment today he remains suspicious with fleeting thought disorder and continuing third-person auditory hallucinations that he describes as the same voices as in the community. Sleep and mood are unremarkable. He has no personal or family psychiatric history. Since admission he has abstained from cannabis (verified by nursing observation and repeat negative urine drug screen 48 hours ago) and has received one dose of olanzapine 10 mg on admission but nothing since due to being suspicious of medication.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 84/min, blood pressure 122/76 mmHg, respiratory rate 16/min, SpO2 99 percent on room air, temperature 36.7 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Alert but suspicious, thought disorder present, persistent third-person auditory hallucinations, no formal thought insertion or withdrawal
data_table.Investigations: Urine drug screen admission cannabinoids only; repeat drug screen 48 hours ago negative for all substances; FBC, UEC, TSH within normal limits

lead_in: Which of the following best guides the next diagnostic step?

options.text: Diagnose primary schizophrenia now and commence long-acting injectable paliperidone as maintenance therapy today
Continue observation and reassess psychotic symptoms after 1 month of confirmed abstinence to clarify diagnosis
Discharge home now with cannabis harm reduction advice and community mental health follow up in the next 2 weeks
Request magnetic resonance imaging of brain today to exclude organic cause as an exclusion diagnosis step
Commence clozapine now for cannabis-induced psychosis that is not responding to a standard antipsychotic trial

subtopic_detail: Reintroducing antipsychotic treatment after catatonia has resolved
stem: A 24-year-old man with schizophrenia developed catatonia while taking haloperidol. It resolved over a week on lorazepam, but his persecutory delusions and thought disorder have returned.

data_table.Examination: Mental state: guarded, persecutory delusions, formal thought disorder, no catatonic signs

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Introduce low dose olanzapine while continuing the lorazepam
Restart haloperidol at half his previous dose with lorazepam
Continue lorazepam alone and defer any antipsychotic for now
Refer for electroconvulsive therapy rather than an antipsychotic
Commence a long-acting injectable antipsychotic at this review

stem:
A 26-year-old man is admitted to your consultation-liaison psychiatry service under the mental health team after 3 days of mutism, refusal to eat and rigid posturing in his outpatient community rehabilitation home. He has known schizoaffective disorder well maintained on aripiprazole for 3 years without prior episodes of catatonia. His family denies illicit substance use in the last month and there has been no recent medication change.

On examination he is alert but immobile with waxy flexibility, echolalia when direct questions are repeated and periods of stereotyped facial grimacing. He resists positioning of his arms after a delay. His vital signs are stable. Full blood count, urea and electrolytes, creatine kinase, thyroid function and urine drug screen are within normal limits. Non-contrast computed tomography of the head is unremarkable. He has a documented allergy to haloperidol (dystonia) but no benzodiazepine history.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 88/min, blood pressure 118/74 mmHg, respiratory rate 16/min, SpO2 99 percent on room air, temperature 36.8 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Mute, waxy flexibility, echolalia when questions repeated, stereotyped grimacing, delayed resistance to passive positioning
data_table.Investigations: FBC, UEC, CK, TFTs and urine drug screen within normal limits; non-contrast CT head unremarkable

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate next diagnostic and therapeutic step?

options.text: Administer intravenous lorazepam 2 mg and reassess the Bush-Francis Catatonia Rating Scale after 10 to 15 minutes
Commence intravenous haloperidol 5 mg immediately for behavioural containment and psychosis in the same dose interval
Arrange urgent electroconvulsive therapy this afternoon without further trial of pharmacological treatment first
Start intravenous dantrolene 2.5 mg per kilogram to treat suspected neuroleptic malignant syndrome as first therapy
Initiate intravenous olanzapine 10 mg with intramuscular midazolam sedation to manage acute behavioural presentation

subtopic_detail: Choosing an antidepressant after an overdose of one
stem: A 27-year-old woman has recovered fully after an amitriptyline overdose taken during a depressive episode. She has no cardiac history, wants to continue antidepressant treatment, and is being discharged to her general practitioner and the community mental health team.

data_table.Examination: Alert, GCS 15, no delirium
data_table.ECG: Sinus rhythm, QRS 86 ms, QTc 410 ms
data_table.Mental state: Mood improving, regrets the act, no current intent

lead_in: Which antidepressant is most appropriate?

options.text: Sertraline with early community review
Amitriptyline with early community review
Nortriptyline with early community review
Venlafaxine with early community review
Phenelzine with early community review

stem:
A 28-year-old software engineer presents to your general practice requesting an ADHD assessment. She reports lifelong difficulty finishing tasks, chronic procrastination and losing personal items, dating back to primary school reports of daydreaming in class. She has managed academically but describes constant last-minute crisis work and increasing job stress. She has one previous episode of major depression 5 years ago that responded to sertraline for 12 months and no other psychiatric history. She drinks 10 standard drinks per week and does not use illicit substances.

On examination she is well groomed and organised for the appointment. Mental state is euthymic with no psychosis and no active suicidality. Her physical examination and vital signs are unremarkable. She has brought school reports and a parent-completed retrospective report scored as suggestive of childhood inattentive presentation. She has no personal history of cardiovascular disease and no family history of sudden cardiac death.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 74/min, blood pressure 118/72 mmHg, respiratory rate 16/min, SpO2 99 percent on room air, temperature 36.7 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Well groomed, euthymic mental state, no thought disorder, insight preserved, no cardiovascular findings
data_table.Investigations: Not required today

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate next step in her assessment?

options.text: Commence a trial of methylphenidate 10 mg twice daily to observe symptomatic response and confirm the diagnosis on treatment
Order neuropsychological testing today and interpret the results in general practice before further specialist referral
Refer to a consultant psychiatrist with a specific interest in adult ADHD for structured diagnostic interview and stimulant authority
Reintroduce sertraline 50 mg daily and reassess in 6 to 8 weeks assuming the current picture is depressive relapse
Provide reassurance that her presentation is common workplace stress and recommend cognitive behavioural therapy alone as sufficient care

stem:
A 19-year-old university student is brought to your urgent care clinic by his housemates after 5 days of paranoid beliefs that Australian Security Intelligence Organisation agents are surveilling him through his laptop camera. He has been using high-potency edible cannabis products daily for 4 months, most recently increasing to twice daily. He has no personal or family psychiatric history. His father has type 2 diabetes but there are no other medical conditions.

On examination he is anxious but engageable, oriented to time, place and person. Speech is coherent but pressured. He describes persecutory delusions and reports hearing his neighbours talk about him through the walls when they are demonstrably away at work. Insight is limited. Physical examination is unremarkable with a mildly elevated heart rate. Urine drug screen is positive for tetrahydrocannabinol only. Full blood count, urea and electrolytes, thyroid function and non-contrast computed tomography head are within normal limits. He has never seen a psychiatrist before.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 108/min, blood pressure 128/78 mmHg, respiratory rate 18/min, SpO2 99 percent on room air, temperature 37.0 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Anxious, oriented, pressured coherent speech, persecutory delusions, third-person auditory hallucinations, limited insight
data_table.Investigations: Urine drug screen positive for THC only; FBC, UEC, TFTs and CT head within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial pharmacological and disposition plan?

options.text: Discharge home with 3 days of oral diazepam 5 mg three times daily to manage cannabis withdrawal only and no antipsychotic
Commence oral clozapine 12.5 mg titrated up over 2 weeks as first-line antipsychotic for treatment-resistant psychosis
Admit involuntarily under the Mental Health Act and commence intramuscular depot risperidone microspheres 25 mg fortnightly from day 1
Refer for admission to a voluntary early psychosis inpatient bed, commence oral olanzapine 5 to 10 mg nightly and support cessation of cannabis
Commence lithium carbonate 500 mg twice daily as mood stabiliser assuming underlying bipolar disorder with psychotic features

stem:
A 26-year-old woman with bipolar I disorder is reviewed in your outpatient psychiatry clinic. She has been stable for 3 years on sodium valproate 1200 mg daily after two prior manic episodes with psychotic features. She is in a new relationship with her partner of 6 months and has stopped her copper intrauterine device 2 weeks ago because they are planning pregnancy in the next year. She has no other medical conditions and does not use any other prescribed or over-the-counter medications.

On examination she is euthymic with no evidence of mood elevation or depression, no psychotic symptoms and preserved insight. She reports adherence with valproate and finds it effective. She has never been prescribed lithium or lamotrigine. Her last serum valproate level was 84 mg/L (50-100). Full blood count, urea and electrolytes, liver enzymes and thyroid function are within normal limits. She is now asking whether she can continue valproate through pregnancy.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 68/min, blood pressure 118/70 mmHg, respiratory rate 16/min, SpO2 99 percent on room air, temperature 36.8 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Euthymic, no psychotic symptoms, insight preserved, no tremor, no gait disturbance
data_table.Investigations: Serum valproate 84 mg/L (50-100); FBC, UEC, LFTs and TFTs within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management of her mood stabiliser?

options.text: Continue valproate 1200 mg daily and add folic acid 5 mg daily preconception to reduce fetal neural tube defect risk
Reduce valproate to 500 mg daily as a below-threshold dose that avoids teratogenicity while planning pregnancy
Continue valproate throughout pregnancy but arrange first-trimester detailed anomaly ultrasound as risk mitigation only
Stop valproate and add quetiapine 300 mg nightly as monotherapy indefinitely and defer any pregnancy planning for 3 years
Wean valproate and cross-titrate to lithium 750 mg nightly, aiming for a serum lithium 0.6 to 0.8 mmol/L before conception

stem:
A 42-year-old man with treatment-resistant schizophrenia has been on clozapine 400 mg nightly for 18 months with excellent symptom response and metabolic side effects only. His routine haematological monitoring today shows an absolute neutrophil count of 1.2 x10^9/L (2.0-7.5), white cell count of 3.4 x10^9/L (4.0-11.0), platelets of 190 x10^9/L (150-400) and haemoglobin of 138 g/L (130-170). He is asymptomatic, afebrile and his mother says he has been better than she has ever seen him. He has never received granulocyte colony-stimulating factor.

On examination he is well, alert, oriented and stable. Vital signs are normal. There are no signs of infection, no oral ulceration and no rash. Prior monitoring bloods have shown ANC consistently 2.5 to 4.0 x10^9/L. He lives independently in supported accommodation with weekly community mental health nurse visits. He is not of Aboriginal or Torres Strait Islander background and no benign ethnic neutropenia has been documented.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 78/min, blood pressure 128/78 mmHg, respiratory rate 16/min, SpO2 99 percent on room air, temperature 36.7 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Well, alert, oriented, no infection focus, no oral ulceration, no rash

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management step?

options.text: Continue clozapine at the current dose and repeat the full blood count with differential within 24 hours to trend the neutrophil count
Stop clozapine immediately and admit for daily full blood count monitoring until ANC recovers above 3.0 x10^9/L
Continue clozapine at reduced dose 200 mg nightly for the next fortnight and repeat full blood count monthly instead of weekly
Commence subcutaneous filgrastim 300 micrograms daily as prophylactic G-CSF before any dose or monitoring change
Cease clozapine permanently and cross-titrate to intramuscular paliperidone palmitate 100 mg monthly given the risk of agranulocytosis

subtopic_detail: Serotonin syndrome vs neuroleptic malignant syndrome
stem:
A 45-year-old man with schizoaffective disorder is brought to your emergency department by his wife after 6 hours of confusion, agitation and shaking. He had olanzapine 15 mg nightly for 5 years without change. Three days ago his general practitioner prescribed venlafaxine 75 mg daily for a superimposed depressive episode; he took his first dose 3 days ago, has escalated with an extra tablet on his own initiative today. This afternoon he also took 2 tablets of tramadol 50 mg for back pain, and one of his wife's linezolid tablets for a chest infection because he assumed it would help.

On examination he is diaphoretic, agitated and disoriented to time. His tone is markedly increased in the lower limbs with clonus at both ankles far exceeding the upper limbs, and hyperactive tendon reflexes throughout. Pupils are dilated at 6 mm and reactive. There is mild rigidity but no lead-pipe rigidity of the upper limbs. Creatine kinase is 780 U/L (30-200), sodium 138 mmol/L (135-145), venous pH 7.30, and urine drug screen is negative for stimulants.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 138/min, blood pressure 168/102 mmHg, respiratory rate 24/min, SpO2 97 percent on room air, temperature 39.2 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Diaphoretic, agitated, disoriented, lower limb clonus greater than upper limb, hyperreflexia, dilated reactive pupils, mild rigidity without lead-pipe
data_table.Investigations: CK 780 U/L (30-200); sodium 138 mmol/L (135-145); venous pH 7.30; urine drug screen negative for stimulants

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate immediate management step?

options.text: Intravenous dantrolene 2.5 mg per kilogram as first-line antidote for neuroleptic malignant syndrome from long-term olanzapine
Cease all serotonergic drugs, give intravenous benzodiazepine sedation and consider oral cyproheptadine 12 mg loading dose then 2 mg every 2 hours
Intramuscular bromocriptine 2.5 mg as a dopamine agonist to reverse suspected neuroleptic malignant syndrome caused by olanzapine
Restart oral olanzapine at reduced dose 5 mg immediately to control agitation and consider ECT if response is inadequate
Intravenous 8.4 percent sodium bicarbonate 2 mmol per kilogram bolus targeting an arterial pH of 7.50 for suspected cardiotoxicity
